# Devadaha Sutta (MN 101 (PTS MN ii 214))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Devadaha Sutta* (MN 101, PTS MN ii 214) is a discourse set in connection with the Sakyan town of Devadaha, though traditional commentaries state that it was spoken at Lumbini while the Buddha was traveling between Kapilavatthu and Devadaha [Dhammika; SuttaCentral]. In this sutta, the Buddha directly challenges a group of Nigaṇṭha (Jain) ascetics who practice rigorous self-mortification—such as standing erect, refusing to sit, and enduring acute, racking pain (*opakkamikā dukkhā tippā kaṭukā vedanā*)—in the belief that all pleasant, painful, or neutral experience is caused by past actions (*sabbaṁ taṁ pubbekatahetu*) and must be purged through austerity [MacQueen 1988; Polak 2011; SuttaCentral]. Exposing logical fallacies in this view, the Buddha points out through two-cornered questions that the ascetics have no direct knowledge of their past deeds or how much karma remains to be eradicated, relying solely on Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's claim to omniscience [Appleton; Hegoda Khemananda 1993]. The discourse emphasizes that present experience is not wholly pre-determined, thereby preserving moral responsibility and the efficacy of present effort, before expounding the Buddha's own gradual training and middle way [Bodhi 1970; Farrington; Kalupahana 1986; SuttaCentral]. The text also contains the simile of a man relinquishing attachment to a woman, which is later cited in the *Visuddhimagga* to illustrate the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*) [Anālayo 2010].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify the direct Chinese Āgama counterpart as MĀ 19 in the *Madhyama Āgama* (translated by Gautama Saṅghadeva) [Kalupahana 1986; SuttaCentral]. In the Pali tradition, significant shared material and parallel formulations occur in texts such as the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta* (MN 14), *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), AN 4.198, and AN 10.99 [Polak 2011; SuttaCentral]. Computational analysis via DharmaNexus confirms this extensive Pali reuse, showing long matching segments between MN 101 and AN 10 (§§30.1–38.2 ↔ AN 10.99), AN 4 (§§30.1–38.2 ↔ AN 4.198), DN 2, and MN 14 (§§4.2–5.7) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages of MN 101 with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and various Tibetan and Sanskrit canonical and Mahāyāna treatises [DharmaNexus].
